limitations_and_boundaries: HaCaT cells showed stronger correlation with −1/2 defects, possibly due to multi-stratified organization and higher elasticity.
Caspase-3 activation only occurred when there was an extrusion; inhibition eliminated extrusions but defect density was maintained.
Cell division inhibition did not alter extensile nature of MDCK.
Extrusion–defect spatial correlation slightly reduced under blebbistatin treatment, suggesting stress regulation through actomyosin activity.
The study primarily uses MDCK cells; other epithelial types tested but with limited sample sizes.
The mechanism is proposed for apoptotic extrusion; other extrusion types (e.g., oncogenic) not directly tested.
The selected source chunks do not report a rescue, reconstitution, reversal, or epistasis experiment; that rung of the causal evidence chain remains untested within this extraction scope.

methods.name: Automated nematic characterization
methods.protocol_description: Phase contrast or fluorescence images smoothed with Bandpass Filter; OrientationJ used to detect direction of largest eigenvector of structure tensor; local nematic order parameter tensor Q calculated; defects detected by winding number; only stably detected defects (≥2 consecutive frames) considered.

results.metric_name: Extrusion correlation with defects across cell types

provenance.text_excerpt: We further found similar extrusion–defect links in different types of epithelium (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1e–h), including a cell-division-inhibited (treated with mytomycin C) MDCK monolayer, a breast cell line (MCF10A) and human epithelial skin (HaCaT). In the last case, we found a correlation between extrusions and defects, but with a stronger correlation with −1/2 defects, which may be attributed to the multi-stratified organization of HaCaT cells as well as the HaCaT cell layers being more elastic than the MDCK monolayer.

results.value_raw_text: Similar extrusion–defect links found in MDCK (WT and mytomycin C treated), MCF10A, and HaCaT; HaCaT showed stronger correlation with −1/2 defects.

provenance.text_excerpt: The isotropic stress provides a clear distinction between +1/2 and −1/2 defects as it is only highly compressive (negative) at the head portion of a +1/2 defect, while being more tensile at a −1/2 defect (Fig. 3a, Experiment).

results.value_raw_text: Isotropic stress is highly compressive (negative) at the head of +1/2 defects, while more tensile at −1/2 defects.

provenance.text_excerpt: We observed that there were substantially more cells at the head region of +1/2 defects than in −1/2 defect cores that had YAP sequestered in their cytoplasm (Fig. 3d, e).

results.value_raw_text: Substantially more cells at the head region of +1/2 defects had YAP sequestered in their cytoplasm compared to −1/2 defect cores or random points.

provenance.text_excerpt: We then measured the time evolution of the average isotropic stress for cells that were going to extrude, and found that such cells were being increasingly compressed (increasingly negative isotropic stress with time, see Fig. 3b) in the time leading up to their extrusion. Notably, the time at which stress started to become more compressive (about −110 min) was consistent with the start of the long-range flow and with the rise in the defect–extrusion correlation.

results.value_raw_text: Cells destined to extrude experienced increasingly negative isotropic stress (compression) starting around −110 min, with significant compression at later time points.

provenance.text_excerpt: Altogether, these results confirm that the epithelium is behaving as an active nematic liquid crystal and that topological defects are spontaneously formed by active stresses in the monolayer.
